en: May the Unmanifest Upaniṣad— the lion of self-knowledge that devours the demon-king of one's own ignorance—
make me Brahman alone, entirely free from all opposites.
Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, and likewise strength and all my senses swell. May everything be the Upaniṣad of Brahman;
may I not deny Brahman, and may Brahman not deny me—this is non-denial.
May there be no obstruction to my head; may that [peace] be mine as I am devoted to the Self. May those virtues which are in the Upanishads abide in me; may they abide in me. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Hari Om! In the beginning, it is said, this was nothing at all; there was neither heaven, nor mid-air, nor earth.
There was only the form of light—beginningless and endless, neither minute nor gross, formless yet possessing form, unknowable, consisting of knowledge, and composed of bliss.
That which was non-different from it became twofold: one was green and the other was red. Of these, that which was red became the form of the Puruṣa; that which was green became the form of Māyā.
They united, and their seed rejoiced. It grew.
Then that golden egg came into being.
As it was undergoing transformation, from it Parameṣṭhin was born. He desired to know: "What is my lineage? What is my duty? Then Speech, though invisible, addressed him: "Oho! O Prajāpati!"
"You have arisen from the unmanifest; your task is the manifest. "What is that unmanifest from which I have arisen? What is that manifest which is my task?
She replied, "For that splendor, O gentle one, is indeed unknowable. That which is unknowable is the unmanifest."

"If you wish to know that, do not understand it [from me]. He said, "Who are you that you are this voice of Brahman? Declare yourself. She replied, "Seek to know me through austerity. He lived as a student of sacred knowledge for a thousand years; he lived [there]. || 1 ||

Then he beheld the Anuṣṭubh verse, the supreme knowledge, of which all other mantras are but limbs; wherein Brahman is established, and wherein all the gods are established. He who does not know that—what is the use of other Vedas?
He will do so. Having understood her, he desired to test his passion for her.
He sat singing to her as she recited in this manner; for a thousand years, he sang the verses with the syllable *oṃ* placed at both the beginning and the end. For a thousand [years...]

He saw [the Lord] exactly as he had been described, syllable by syllable; then he beheld Him, composed of light, embraced by Śrī, seated upon the chariot of Suparṇa, His head shaded by the hoods of Śeṣa,
with the face of a deer and the body of a man, possessing three eyes consisting of the moon, the sun, and the sacrificial fire.
Then Prajāpati prostrated himself, saying "Salutation after salutation. He then praised him with the Ṛgvedic verse.

He said, "The Fierce (ugra)," for he is indeed fierce because of his form as a deer. He said, "The Hero (vīra)," for he is indeed a hero because of his prowess. He said, "Mahāviṣṇu," for he belongs to the great.
He stands pervading the great heaven and earth. Regarding "blazing," he says that indeed he stands as if blazing.
Regarding "facing in all directions," he says that indeed he possesses faces on all sides because of his universal form (*viśvarūpa*).
Regarding "Nṛsiṃha," he says this is just like the Yajus mantra. Regarding "terrifying," he says it is because of fear...
From him the sun rises; the moon shines in fear; the wind blows in fear; fire burns in fear;

Parjanya rains in fear. He says, "Auspiciousness," for he is indeed auspicious and endowed with glory. He says, "Death from death," for he is indeed the death of death, [granting] immortality to creatures who consume food.
"I bow," he says; this is just like a sacrificial formula (yajus). "I," he says; this is just like a sacrificial formula. || 2 ||

Then the Blessed One said to him, "O Prajāpati, I am pleased; what is desired by you? Ask for that. He replied, "Blessed One, it was heard by me of old that I have arisen from the Unmanifest (avyakta) and my task is the Manifest (vyakta). In that regard, it was understood that you are the Unmanifest."
"Tell me clearly," he said. "The manifest (vyakta) is indeed the universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
That which is manifested is the manifestness of the manifest. He replied, "I am not able to create the world; tell me the means. To him, the Puruṣa said, "O Prajāpati..."
Listen to the supreme means of creation, knowing which you will know everything;

you will be capable in all things and shall accomplish all. One should meditate upon one's own self as the oblation in the fire that is I, by means of that very Anuṣṭubh verse. This indeed is the sacrifice of meditation.

This indeed is the Great Upaniṣad, the secret of the gods. Truly, for one who knows this, there is no purpose whatsoever served by the Sāman, the Ṛc, or the Yajus. Having attained all desires and conquered all worlds, he comes unto me alone; he who knows thus does not return again. Thus [ends the third section].

Prajāpati, considering himself superior through this sacrifice, performed a mental sacrifice (*manoyajña*). Having meditated upon the oblation with that very *ṛc* accompanied by the *praṇava*, he offered himself into the fire within his own self. He understood everything, he was capable of everything, and he accomplished everything.

He who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice of meditation becomes omniscient, possessed of infinite power, and the creator of all. Having conquered all worlds, he attains the supreme Brahman. || 4 ||

Then Prajāpati, desiring to create the worlds, from the thirty syllables of that very *ṛc* created the three worlds. Then, with two syllables each, he supported them on both sides. From the thirty-two syllables of that same *ṛc*, [he created...]
From her he fashioned the gods; by all of them together, he became Indra. Therefore, Indra became superior to the gods. He who knows thus shall become superior among his equals.
With eleven feet of hers, he fashioned the eleven Rudras. Of her...
With eleven [syllables] he fashioned the eleven Ādityas; with all of them, he became Viṣṇu.
Therefore, Viṣṇu became superior to the Ādityas. He who knows this shall become superior among his equals. With four syllables each, he generated the eight Vasus.
With its first twelve syllables, it generated the Brāhmaṇa;
with ten each, the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is preeminent.
Thus does he become preeminent who knows this.

He silently procreated the Śūdra; therefore, the Śūdra is devoid of sacred knowledge (*nirvidya*). There was neither day nor night, for there was no distinction. That Prajāpati, by means of two half-verses of the *Ānuṣṭubh* meter, fashioned day and night.
Then he desired; verily it rises up for him. Moreover, he drives away the darkness.
He fashioned the Ṛgveda from her first foot, the Yajurveda from the second, the Sāmaveda from the third, and the Atharvāṅgirases from the fourth—namely, that which consists of eight-syllable feet.

By that it is the *gāyatrī*; because it has eleven feet, it is the *triṣṭubh*; because it has four feet, it is the *jagatī*; and because it has thirty-two syllables, it is the *anuṣṭubh*. Indeed, this [Vāk] is all the meters. He who knows her as all the meters—
The entire world has arisen from the *anuṣṭubh* alone; he who knows this finds his firm foundation in the *anuṣṭubh*. || 5 ||

Then, when the created beings did not multiply, Prajāpati, reflecting, "How indeed might I create these beings? began to sing this verse, "Ugram" (The Fierce One). From its first quarter, the deity in his fierce form [emerged].
A single dark-complexioned being appeared before him, red and wielding a bow; dividing himself into male and female forms, he assigned his female form to women and his male form to men.
By these two portions, everything was ordained, and from them, living beings were produced.

He who knows this—Prajāpati, that three-eyed one, too, sang forth this Ṛc while his mass of matted locks was still unbraided, thinking, "May he find delight in the Self alone, which is the inner light.
Now, it is said that Indra was the youngest of the gods; Prajāpati said to him, "Go!"

"Be the sovereign of the gods. He went there. The gods said to him, "You are the youngest among us; how can you have sovereignty? He approached Prajāpati and said, "The gods spoke thus: 'You are the youngest; how can you have sovereignty? Prajāpati [spoke] to that Indra.

Having consecrated him with three water-pots filled with nectar and empowered by the *ānuṣṭubha* mantra, he protected him from the right with the *sudarśana* discus and from the left with the *pāñcajanya* conch; thus, he became well-protected by these two alone. Upon a golden tablet radiant as the sun, [he inscribed] the *ānuṣṭubha* mantra.
Having placed it upon his neck, he fastened it; thereupon he became difficult to look upon.

He bestowed upon him the Ānuṣṭubh Vidyā. Then the gods consented to his sovereignty. He became self-ruling (*svarāṭ*). Whoever knows thus shall become self-ruling. He thought [of taking] even the earth.
"How may I conquer the waters? he thought, and he ran to Prajāpati.
Therefore, Prajāpati gave him a throne in the form of a tortoise, supported by Indra, the Nāgas, and the lords of serpents. He conquered the earth. Then he...

He became the sovereign of both worlds. He who knows thus becomes the sovereign of both worlds. He conquers the earth—he who knows thus, and he who knows thus—whoever, being more prosperous than his brothers, is unestablished and unstable. 6.
Whoever studies this knowledge studies all the Vedas; he sacrifices with all the sacrificial rites;
he bathes in all the sacred fords; he is liberated from great and minor sins;
he shall attain great spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); [he remembers] the ancestors from Brahmā back through the past kalpas and those who come after.

He purifies his lineage. Diseases such as epilepsy shall not afflict him. Even those who are possessed by yakṣas, or who are ghosts and piśācas, upon touching, seeing, or hearing him, shall become virtuous and attain the holy worlds. All his goals are accomplished merely by his thinking of them.
They shall attain perfection. All regard him as they would their own father. Kings become obedient to his commands.
He should not offer salutations upon seeing anyone superior to himself other than his teacher (*ācārya*).
Nor should he descend from this state. He becomes liberated while yet living (*jīvanmukta*), and at the end of the body, [he goes] beyond darkness.

One shall attain that abode where Virāṭ Nṛsiṃha shines forth; there indeed do they worship. Devoted to meditation on His true nature, the sages merge into that very Self until the end of the kalpa, and they do not return again. One should not speak this knowledge to one who lacks faith, nor to one who is envious.

It is not for one who has not studied the Vedas, nor for one who is not a devotee of Viṣṇu, nor for a liar, nor for one who lacks austerity, nor for one who is undisciplined, nor for one who is not tranquil, nor for one who is uninitiated, nor for one whose character is unrighteous, nor for a harmful person, nor for one who does not observe celibacy— this is the secret teaching (upaniṣad).
Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and likewise strength and all my senses swell with vigor. May everything be the Upaniṣad of Brahman;
may I not deny Brahman, and may Brahman not deny me—this is non-denial.

May there be no obstruction to my head; may that [state] be in me who am devoted to the Self. Whatever virtues are in the Upanishads, may they be in me; may they be in me. Om. Peace, peace, peace. Hariḥ Om Tat Sat.
Thus ends the Avyakta Upaniṣad.
